subject: ent
title: Acute otitis media and otitis media with effusion

steps.tx: **Acute otitis media** is middle ear infection behind an intact drum, peaking in young children whose short horizontal Eustachian tubes admit nasopharyngeal bacteria after viral colds. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis dominate. Otalgia, fever, a bulging red drum and lost landmarks make the diagnosis; a merely red drum in a crying child does not.
steps.say: Toddlers get middle ear infections after colds through short Eustachian tubes. Bulging drum plus pain and fever diagnose it, not mere redness.

steps.tx: **Key point.** Most acute otitis media resolves spontaneously, so guidelines use analgesia and watchful waiting for mild older cases, with antibiotics for infants, bilateral, severe or otorrhoea cases (local protocol decides agents). Decongestants and antihistamines do not help. Persistent bulge risks perforation, which paradoxically relieves pain as pus drains.
steps.say: Many ear infections settle alone. Pain relief first; antibiotics for young, bilateral or severe cases. Nasal sprays do not clear middle ears.

steps.tx: **Otitis media with effusion (glue ear)** is sterile fluid behind an intact drum without acute infection, causing conductive deafness, speech delay and school difficulty in children. The drum looks dull, retracted or with visible fluid level and bubbles. Most effusions clear in three months, so watchful waiting precedes intervention.
steps.say: Glue ear is quiet fluid deafening children without infection. Most clears within three months, so watch before operating.

steps.tx: Persistent bilateral effusion with hearing loss beyond three months, speech or developmental impact, leads to hearing tests and consideration of **ventilation tubes (grommets)**, which equalise pressure while inserted but extrude spontaneously. Adenoidectomy helps selected older children with nasal obstruction. Autoinflation devices aid some cooperative children.
steps.say: Lasting glue ear with deafness earns hearing tests and possible grommets. Tubes fall out alone. Big adenoids blocking the nose may need removal too.

rows: Watch 3 months, then tubes if deaf

steps.tx: **Key point.** Recurrent acute otitis media (three in six months or four in a year) prompts ENT referral, hearing assessment and risk reduction: smoke free home, breastfeeding support and pneumococcal vaccination status. Effusion in an adult, especially unilateral, mandates nasopharyngeal examination to exclude obstructing tumour, a classic exam trap.
steps.say: Repeated infections need referral and hearing checks. One sided glue ear in an adult means examine the nasopharynx for tumour.
